lines.text: You cut an onion. Seconds later, you're crying. That's the onion fighting back.
An onion's cells keep two things apart: sulphur compounds, and an enzyme.
Your knife breaks the cell walls, and they mix.
That reaction makes a gas, syn-propanethial-S-oxide. Scientists think it evolved to stop animals from eating the onion.
The gas drifts up and reaches your eyes. Nerves there sense the irritation, and your brain sends tears to wash it away.
So those tears aren't sadness. They're a defence system working perfectly.
Want fewer tears? Chill the onion first, because cold slows the gas down. And use a sharp knife, so fewer cells break.
The onion can't run away. So it makes you cry instead.
